title: Brewery data on Google Cloud, read where it already sits
standfirst: If your sales, e-commerce or group reporting already lives on Google Cloud, you do not need to move it. Beer365 reads BigQuery and Cloud Storage and joins them to the brewing side.
description: Brewery data on Google Cloud: Beer365 reads BigQuery and Cloud Storage where they sit and joins them to brewing data, with no migration of your stack.

sections.h2: Why breweries on Google Cloud get stuck

blocks.p: Breweries usually arrive on Google Cloud through the commercial side. E-commerce, distributor portals, marketing and sales reporting land in BigQuery because that is where the analytics team was comfortable. The production side lives somewhere else: brew sheets in Excel, the historian on site, the ERP in its own database.

So the forecast can be right and the beer can still be missing from the warehouse. The sales data knows what will sell. It does not know that the wheat beer needed for festival week is still in a fermenter, or that the bright tank it needs is booked for something else. That gap is not a cloud problem. It is a join nobody has made.

The usual answer from a provider is to move everything into one cloud first. That puts a year of migration between the brewery and its first useful number. The commercial team loses tools that work. The brewing side waits. We think the order should be the other way round: answer the question first, on the data where it sits.

Say a brewery sells a wheat beer that averages 800 hL a week. Three years of sales history show demand rising for a regional festival. The forecast for festival week is 1,200 hL. Stock on hand is 3,000 hL.

eq.label: Weeks of stock cover
eq.code: cover (weeks) = stock on hand / forecast weekly demand = 3,000 hL / 1,200 hL = 2.5 weeks
eq.note: At the normal 800 hL a week the same stock reads as 3,000 / 800 = 3.75 weeks.

blocks.p: The gap between 3.75 and 2.5 weeks is the gap between a relaxed planner and a brewhouse that should have brewed a fortnight ago. A wheat beer brewed today will not be packaged for a couple of weeks at best. The forecast only helps if it sits next to tank availability and the brewing plan, in front of the person who decides what to brew next.

The forecast is also only as honest as its history. If a stock-out week is recorded as low demand, the forecast learns that festivals are quieter than they are. How to treat those weeks is a sales and supply chain decision. Your people sign it off, not ours.

That is what the brewery decides differently once the two sides meet. The planner sees cover by SKU against the date each tank will be free. Sales sees which outlets will run short. Finance sees what a missed festival week costs in hectolitres not sold.

sections.h2: How Beer365 reads Google Cloud data

blocks.p: Beer365 runs on Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Fabric inside your own Microsoft tenant. It reaches Google Cloud in two ways, chosen per source.

head: Where the data sits
How Beer365 reads it
What your IT team should know
rows: A read-only OneLake shortcut that points at the bucket
Nothing is copied by default. Access uses an HMAC key for an account with read and list rights on the bucket. Fabric can cache files for 1 to 28 days to cut repeated egress.

A copy kept in step with BigQuery, typically about ten minutes behind. Microsoft does not charge Fabric compute for the replication. Storage is free up to a limit set by capacity. BigQuery's own change tracking and storage costs still apply on the Google side.

blocks.p: The choice between the two is practical. Tables that already live in BigQuery, such as depletions by outlet, suit mirroring. Files in buckets, such as distributor sales drops or historian exports, suit a shortcut. Either way the brewing side, read from Excel, the ERP, SCADA, the historian and the LIMS, joins the same batch record inside your tenant. Nothing is written back to any of them.

One point to plan for. Security rules set inside BigQuery do not travel with a mirror. They are set again in Fabric, matching the rules you already have, as part of the proof of concept. The work is small. Forgetting it is not.

sections.h2: Questions to ask any provider when you run on Google Cloud

ul: **Does it need a migration?** If it does, ask what that gives the brewery that reading in place does not.
**Is each source copied or read in place?** Both are fine. You should know which, source by source.
**How current will it be?** A mirror about ten minutes behind is fine for planning. It is not an alarm.
**Who rebuilds the security rules?** Mirrored tables do not inherit BigQuery permissions.
**What will it cost on both sides?** Google charges for egress and change tracking. Microsoft charges for capacity.
**Who owns the batch record at the end?** It should already sit in your tenant.

sections.h2: How Beer365 delivers it alongside Google Cloud

ul: **Assessment, two weeks, fixed price.** We list what sits in BigQuery and Cloud Storage, what sits on site and which question links them first, for example stock cover against tank availability.
**Proof of concept, 20 weeks.** The batch record joins brewing and commercial data for that question against a baseline signed at the start. Your plant controller signs a statement every month.
**Live.** More sources and roles join the same record, with the Power BI pages, the digital twin and the copilot reading from it.

blocks.p: From IT we need a read-only key on the relevant buckets, access to the BigQuery tables to mirror, a Microsoft tenant with Fabric capacity and a named contact. You own every report, model and record. Your Google Cloud stack stays exactly where it is.

faq.q: Do we have to leave Google Cloud?
faq.a: No. Beer365 reads Cloud Storage in place through a read-only shortcut and mirrors the BigQuery tables it needs. Your Google Cloud stack stays as it is.
Mirrored tables are. The copy sits in OneLake inside your own tenant, kept in step with BigQuery and typically about ten minutes behind. Files in Cloud Storage are read in place.

faq.q: Will our BigQuery permissions carry over?
faq.a: No. Mirroring does not bring BigQuery's granular security with it. The same rules are set again in Fabric during the proof of concept.

faq.q: Who pays the Google Cloud costs?
faq.a: You do, on your Google account, for egress and BigQuery change tracking. The assessment estimates them alongside the Fabric capacity cost.
